extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, and formal-methods researchers interested in understanding and formalizing mathematical proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing how ordinary mathematical proofs (including algebraic and diagrammatic proofs) license inferences and how those practices can be captured or formalized in proof assistants and philosophical accounts. Emphasis on structural methods, diagram-based reasoning, and managing mixed numeric domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic method — generality
rubrics_metrics.description: A single abstract theorem about groups has consequences everywhere a group can be identified; general arguments are more efficient than repeating ad hoc arguments in each specific setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes generality as the most commonly cited advantage of algebraic methods: carry out a general argument once and apply it across contexts. Example: Proposition 1 (about groups) yields Euler’s theorem and Fermat’s little theorem when specialized. Scoring note: value arguments that identify an abstract structure and apply general theorems rather than rederiving case-specific calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic method — terminological and notational benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic methods often yield terminological and notational conveniences that simplify calculations and manipulations compared to cumbersome locutions in elementary arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes providing concise names and operations that hide repetitive low-level calculations. Example: recognizing multiplicative units modulo m as a group avoids writing explicit calculations for inverses. Anti-pattern: proofs that clutter exposition with low-level computations that an algebraic abstraction would make unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic method — suppression of irrelevant information
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebraic abstraction focuses effort by suppressing distracting information irrelevant to solving the problem; one need only know the existence of structure-relevant facts (e.g. existence of an inverse), not their explicit construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the modular arithmetic proof it suffices to know b1 b2 · · · bn has a multiplicative inverse modulo m; one need not produce the particular inverse. Good practice: isolate the structural fact used and avoid superfluous calculations. Bad practice: over-emphasizing particular representatives when structure alone suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling the 'context' in proof assistants (locales/modules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal verification systems should provide methods for collections of facts and procedures that are 'ready to hand' in a context; Isabelle implements 'locales' and Coq supports 'modules'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems must support identifying theorems as about a structure (e.g. groups), specializing general facts automatically to particular instances, and making those facts available in the local proof context. Example script: Isabelle's (in comm-group) locale and subsequent lemma and theorem usage. Implementation criterion: ensure the system can mark, import, and instantiate relevant facts for a context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bookkeeping and combination of locales/modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanisms are required to manage locales and combine them effectively, because structures instantiate and inherit facts from one another (e.g. every abelian group is a group; multiplicative units of a ring form a group).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal systems need complex bookkeeping to track which facts and procedures are immediately available when recognizing structures embedded in others. Good implementations provide inheritance, composition, and automatic transport of facts; poor implementations force manual re-specification or verification of routine specialization steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure behind concise proof scripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Although proof scripts in systems like Isabelle/Coq may be relatively short, substantial underlying machinery (locales, rewrite rules, calculational rules) is required to make algebraic reasoning work as in textbooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should distinguish between surface concision and the infrastructural effort required. When formalizing textbook-style algebraic proofs, ensure the necessary library support, identification mechanisms, and automations are in place before judging formal proofs as 'simple'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrammatic reasoning — coexact vs exact distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish 'exact' conditions (e.g. two segments are congruent) from 'coexact' conditions (e.g. two lines intersect or a point lies in a given region); coexact conditions depend only on general topological features of the diagram and are stable under perturbations, whereas exact conditions are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manders’ key observation: only coexact claims are ever inferred from a diagram in Euclidean proofs; text assertions are required for inferences that result in exact claims. Good diagrammatic practice: use diagrams to represent coexact data and supply textual justification for exact claims. Anti-pattern: treating exact metric facts as if they were licensed purely by the drawn diagram without textual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal systems for diagram-based reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: A faithful formal system for Euclidean reasoning should have diagrams and formulas together represent assertions, with precise rules governing diagram construction and allowable inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two approaches: Miller treats diagrams as abstract graphs encoding topological data; Mumma represents diagrams as labeled geometric elements with coordinates on a point grid. Criterion for such systems: (i) explicit representation of diagrammatic data, (ii) formal rules for which diagrammatic inferences are licensed, (iii) validation mechanisms for those inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validating generality from particular diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof begins with a particular diagram (e.g. triangle ABC) it must provide a justification of why reasoning about that particular case yields conclusions valid for all configurations (avoiding illicit dependence on accidental features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two validation strategies: (a) Miller's approach — carry out case splits for each topological configuration that can arise (complete but may explode combinatorially); (b) Mumma's approach — provide rules that justify certain diagram features as general consequences of the construction, independent of particular choices. Good proofs either handle all relevant cases or provide rules ensuring irrelevance of representational choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing faithful computational methods for geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern geometric theorem provers often use algebraic embeddings (e.g. embed Euclidean geometry into the Cartesian plane and use decision procedures for real closed fields), but one may prefer methods that verify Euclidean inferences on their own (diagrammatic) terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate methods for faithfulness to Euclidean practice, scalability, and explanatory power. Algebraic methods are powerful and effective (decision procedures, Wu, Chou), but alternative methods may yield better insight into geometric reasoning and the relation to historical diagrammatic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing mixed numeric domains (embeddings and coercions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofs mix natural numbers, integers, rationals, reals, and complexes, authors/readers must keep track of where elements 'live' and use embeddings/coercions (e.g. real(n) in Isabelle) so operations and orderings are applied to appropriate domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalization requires explicit casting/coercions or mechanisms that automate them reliably. Good practice in formalization: make embedding functions explicit or configure the system's coercion machinery and ensure relevant simplifications/verifications are available to avoid tedious manual proofs. Anti-pattern: assuming implicit type identifications without formal casts, which leads to errors or heavy proof obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility conditions for large-scale mathematical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical constraints in large collaborative mathematics require (1) concise, fully explicit theorems that are rigorously detachable from context; (2) theorems stated structurally so different authors can freely use results without rechecking low-level set-theoretic encodings; (3) methods that handle structures at every level and relate different levels coherently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivated by large projects (e.g. Wiles and the Langlands Program), good mathematical practice demands brief, self-contained theorem statements, structural formulation rather than reliance on particular set-theoretic reductions, and uniform methods across levels (from numbers through functors). Failure to follow these makes collaboration and reuse infeasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity-by-stipulation between structures (practical identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice mathematicians often 'identify' a structure with its image in a larger structure by stipulation (e.g. identifying each real number x with the complex x+0i), treating injections S1 ↣ S2 as identity preserving to make S1 a part of S2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks commonly state 'we identify R with its image in C'; this pragmatic move is acceptable and widespread despite philosophical qualms about 'identity by fiat.' When formalizing or philosophically analyzing practice, document these identifications explicitly; be aware philosophers may demand further justification, but in practice the stipulation supports seamless reasoning across domains.
